text: Come, let us return to the LORD. He has torn us, and he will heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind our wounds.
After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.
Let us know the LORD; let us press on to know him. His coming is as certain as the dawn; he will come to us like the rain, like the spring rains that water the earth.
What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that vanishes early.

So I have hewn them down by the prophets; I have slain them with the words of my mouth, and your judgments go forth like the light.[^1]

[^1]: Some ancient versions read "my judgment goes forth like the light."

versions.text: So I have hewn them down by the prophets; I have slain them with the words of my mouth, and my judgment goes forth like the light.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has a second-person suffix ("your judgments") with a plural noun. Rendering it as "my judgment" follows an ancient variant reading, which should be signaled in a footnote; the plural "judgments" also better reflects the Hebrew noun form.

versions.text:
So I have hewn them down by the prophets; I have slain them with the words of my mouth, and my judgments go forth like the light.[^1]

[^1]: The Hebrew text reads "your judgments"; some ancient versions read "my judgment."
versions.explanation: The main text and the footnote currently contradict each other: the footnote states that the Hebrew reads "your judgments," yet the text prints "my judgments," which is neither the Hebrew (second-person suffix, מִשְׁפָּטֶיךָ) nor the ancient variant (singular "my judgment"). Placing the Hebrew reading "your judgments" in the text and noting the variant in the footnote resolves the inconsistency while preserving the plural noun form of the Hebrew.

text: For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

But like Adam they broke the covenant; there they dealt treacherously with me.[^1]

[^1]: Or "like mere men"; or "at Adam," a place name near the Jordan.

versions.text: But like Adam they broke the covenant; there they dealt treacherously with me.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew phrase is ambiguous (personal name, common noun "humankind," or a place name), and the word "there" in the second half suggests a location. A footnote helps readers without altering the chosen rendering.

text: Gilead is a city of evildoers, stained with blood.
Like bandits lying in ambush, so is the band of priests: they murder on the road to Shechem; yes, they commit outrage.
In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing: there Ephraim plays the whore, and Israel is defiled.
For you also, Judah, a harvest is appointed, when I restore the fortunes of my people.
